1.pericope_label: The men from Judea and the first controversy

schools.summary: Gill says the men came down to Antioch and were not sent by the apostles but came of themselves; who they were is not certain, though that they were judaizing Christians and teachers among them is plain from the account that follows, and according to Epiphanius they were Cerinthus and some of his followers. Calvin sets the episode in the course of Paul and Barnabas's ministry: having endured many combats against the professed enemies of the gospel, they are now declared to have been tried by domestic war, so that their doctrine and ministry should be proved by all means and it might the better appear that they were furnished by God and armed against all the assaults of the world and Satan; it was no small confirmation of their doctrine that, being shaken and battered with so many engines, it stood nevertheless, and its course could not be broken off by so many hindrances. This history he calls most worthy of noting, since though we naturally abhor the cross and all manner of persecution, civil and domestic discord is the more dangerous: when tyrants bend their force and run violently upon men the flesh is afraid and all who are not endued with the spirit of fortitude tremble, yet their consciences are not properly touched with any temptation, this being as it were the fatal estate of the Church; but when it falls out that the brethren go together by the ears and the Church is in an uproar within itself, weak minds must be troubled and faint, especially when the controversy is about doctrine, which alone is the holy bond of brotherly unity. There is nothing, he concludes, which does more damage to the gospel than civil discord, because it does not only pierce and wound weak consciences but also ministers occasion to the wicked to backbite; and we must diligently note the history, that we may know it is no new example if among those who profess the same faith such quarrels arise.

Henry draws the moral from the setting: even when things go on very smoothly and pleasantly in a state or in a church it is folly to be secure and to think the mountain stands strong and cannot be moved, since some uneasiness or other will arise which is not foreseen and cannot be prevented but must be prepared for. If ever there was a heaven upon earth, he says, surely it was in the church at Antioch at this time, when there were so many excellent ministers there and blessed Paul among them, building up that church in its most holy faith.

Clarke's block on this verse is not a comment upon it but an analysis of the chapter's whole course: that certain teachers from Judea insist on the necessity of the converted Gentiles being circumcised; that Paul and Barnabas are sent to Jerusalem to consult the apostles; that they come to Jerusalem and inform the apostles of the conversion of the Gentiles and of the trouble which certain Pharisees had occasioned concerning circumcision; and that the apostles, having assembled to consider the question, hear Peter deliver his opinion first. Wesley's note is a single conjecture, that the men came down from Judea perhaps to supply what they thought Paul and Barnabas had omitted.

Barnes says these were undoubtedly men who had been Jews but were now converted to Christianity, the fact that they were willing to refer the matter in dispute to the apostles and elders showing that they had professedly embraced the Christian religion. The account which follows he calls a record of the first internal dissension which occurred in the Christian church: hitherto they had been struggling against external foes, violent persecutions having raged and fully occupied the attention of Christians, but now the churches were at peace and enjoyed great external prosperity at Antioch, and the great enemy of souls took occasion then, as he has often done in similar circumstances since, to excite contentions in the church itself, so that when external violence could not destroy it an effort was made to secure the same object by internal dissension and strife. The history is particularly important as the record of the first unhappy debate which arose in the bosom of the church, as showing the manner in which such controversies were settled in apostolic times, and as establishing some very important principles respecting the perpetuity of the religious rites of the Jews. He notes also that Judea was a high and hilly region, so that going from it toward the level countries adjacent to the sea was represented as descending. Ellicott says we enter here on the history of the first great controversy in the records of the Christian Church, and that it might have seemed as if the conversion of Cornelius had been accepted as deciding the question now raised again; those who had objected to Peter's conduct in that case were not content to accept the conclusion he drew, and to them it may have seemed the exception that proved the rule. Where signs and wonders came in they may have been content to accept an uncircumcised convert simply on the ground that God had dispensed in such cases with his own law, or they may have urged that continuance in the uncircumcised state after baptism was a wilful transgression which shut men out from the salvation they were seeking; circumcision, they may have said, had been given as an everlasting covenant and had never been formally abrogated, and who were the new teachers that they should change what God had thus established? It is clear, he adds, that they came claiming to speak in the name of James, the bishop of Jerusalem, and though he distinctly repudiates having authorised them, if his Epistle was written shortly before the Council they might rest their case on his own words, that whosoever shall keep the whole Law and yet offend in one point is guilty of all. Robertson takes them for the party of the circumcision in the church at Jerusalem, who had heard of the spread of the gospel among the Gentiles and, since Paul and Barnabas did not come up to Jerusalem, decided to go down to Antioch and attack them there; they volunteered without church action, their activity being disclaimed by the conference, and Paul in Galatians describes them with some heat as false brethren secretly introduced who sneaked in to spy out our liberty. The Judaizers had acquiesced in the case of Cornelius after plain proof by Peter that it was the Lord's doing, but had not agreed to a formal campaign to turn the exception into the rule and to make Christianity mainly Gentile with a few Jews instead of mainly Jewish with a few Gentiles. He holds it reasonably certain that the visit to Jerusalem described in Galatians is the same as this conference, in spite of Ramsay's effort to identify it with the earlier famine visit, since Paul is not giving a list of his visits to Jerusalem but showing his independence of the twelve apostles and his equality with them; Luke gives the outward narrative of events while Galatians shows the private interview with the apostles, which came between the public meeting and the deliberation that follows.

Chrysostom marks a pattern in the narrative: at every step of the right progress in respect of the Gentiles, the beginning is brought in as a matter of necessity. Before this, Peter being found fault with justified himself and said all that he said in the tone of apology, which was what made his words acceptable; then, the Jews having turned away, upon this Paul came to the Gentiles; and here again, seeing another extravagance coming in, the apostle enacts the law.

debates: Who the men from Judea were: Gill reports Epiphanius for Cerinthus and his followers while allowing that it is not certain, Barnes infers from their submission of the case that they were professed Christians, Robertson identifies them with the Jerusalem party of the circumcision acting without church authority, and Ellicott says they claimed the name of James, which he repudiates

Why the question revived after the conversion of Cornelius: Ellicott suggests they treated that case as the exception that proved the rule, or as a dispensation that did not license continuance in uncircumcision, while Robertson makes the objection one of scale, that they would not see the exception turned into a formal campaign

Whether the visit of Galatians is this conference or the earlier famine visit: Robertson holds for this conference against Ramsay, arguing that Paul is not listing his visits but establishing his equality with the twelve, and places the private interview between the public meeting and the deliberation

What kind of trial this was: Calvin insists that domestic discord is more dangerous than persecution, since persecution frightens the flesh without touching the conscience, while Barnes treats it as the enemy's change of tactics once external violence had failed

Where the men's authority came from: Ellicott and Robertson agree that the conference itself disclaims them, but Ellicott traces their argument to a written rule of James while Robertson traces their action to a party decision at Jerusalem
outliers: Gill's report from Epiphanius that the men were Cerinthus and his followers
Robertson's use of Galatians to supply the private interview Luke omits, and his direct disagreement with Ramsay
Ellicott's reconstruction of the Judaizers' own case, that circumcision was an everlasting covenant never formally abrogated
Calvin's maxim that nothing does more damage to the gospel than civil discord
Henry's picture of Antioch as a heaven upon earth immediately before the quarrel
Barnes's geographical note that going from hilly Judea toward the coast was described as descending
Chrysostom's pattern that at every step of the Gentile mission the beginning is brought in as a matter of necessity

2.pericope_label: The dispute at Antioch, the journey up, and the Pharisees who believed

schools.summary: Gill says Paul and Barnabas were the ministers of the uncircumcision and had just returned from preaching the Gospel among the Gentiles with success, and being advocates for them and witnesses of the grace bestowed upon them they opposed the sentiments of these men. Of the sending he says they were either accompanied by some of the brethren of the church part of the way, out of respect to them, or were provided by them with things necessary for their journey. The Pharisees he identifies only as the strictest sect of religion among the Jews. Calvin calls it no small trial that Paul and Barnabas should be haled into a troublesome tumult: there was mischief enough already in the dissension itself, but it is a more cruel mischief when the contention waxes so hot that they are enforced to fight with their brethren as with enemies. Since companions were joined to Paul and Barnabas by the common consent of the Church, who might for duty's sake conduct them, we may gather that all the godly were on their side and never otherwise thought than that the cause was theirs as well as the apostles'. By the word church, he says, Luke means the multitude itself and the whole body, after which he assigns a peculiar place to the apostles and elders, by whom Paul and Barnabas were specially received, the apostles having no certain place of abode at Jerusalem. It is not without cause, he adds, that Luke expresses what kind of men they were who went about to trouble or hinder Paul, even at Jerusalem also, and it is to be thought that the evil flowed from that fountain, Luke now more plainly expressing that the trouble broke out there too.

Clarke says Paul and Barnabas were fully satisfied that God did not design to bring the converted Gentiles under the yoke of circumcision, since they knew that Jesus Christ was the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believed, and therefore they opposed the teaching. Being brought on their way he takes of the members of the Church providing them with all necessaries for their journey, since it does not appear that they had any property of their own; and much stress, he says, is laid on their declaring the conversion of the Gentiles, it being a miracle of God's mercy. The Church that received them he takes for the whole body of Christian believers, the apostles for either the whole or part of the twelve, though we read of none but John, Peter and James, and the elders for those who were officers in the Church under the apostles. The rising up of the Pharisees he takes to be part of the declaration made by Paul and Barnabas to the council, who having stated how God blessed their ministry among the Gentiles proceed to declare how all the good work was likely to be hindered. Wesley says the determination that Paul and Barnabas and certain others should go up to Jerusalem about this question is the journey to which Paul refers when he says he went up by revelation, which is very consistent with the account here, since the Church in sending them might itself be so directed. The reception he glosses as a solemn welcome; of the Pharisees he observes that even believers are apt to retain their former turn of mind and the prejudices derived from it; and the law of Moses he takes for the whole law, both moral and ritual.

Barnes says the word rendered dissension sometimes denotes sedition or intestine war and sometimes earnest and violent disputation or controversy, and that in this place it clearly denotes earnest and warm discussion without implying more. Of the journey he notes that it was customary for the Christians to attend the apostles in their travels, and of the reception at Jerusalem that they were received by the church in a hospitable and friendly manner, acknowledged as Christian brethren and received with Christian kindness, and that they then stated the case. On the rising up of the Pharisees he says it has been doubted whether these are the words of Paul and Barnabas relating what occurred at Antioch, or the words of Luke recording what took place at Jerusalem, and that the correct exposition is probably that which refers it to the latter. Ellicott says the two apostles must obviously have agreed in feeling that the teaching of the Judaisers involved a direct condemnation of all the work in which they saw the triumph of God's grace. The route he traces from Seleucia at the mouth of the Orontes along the coast of Sidon and Tyre and probably Caesarea, and then through Samaria, noting that they might have gone to Joppa and so have avoided the old Canaanite cities and the region of the hated Samaritans. The reception implies to him a general gathering of the Church, members of different synagogues coming together with the elders who presided over them, the position of the apostles being only in some degree analogous. The Pharisees who believed he calls the first distinct mention of the conversion of any of the Pharisaic party, though a drift in that direction had been going on for some time, beginning during our Lord's ministry and showing itself since. Robertson parses the genitive absolute and keeps the litotes of no little dissension and questioning, notes Luke's favourite method of resumptive narrative at the third verse and the old verb for being brought forward on one's way, calls the reception at Jerusalem a public one provided by the whole church including the apostles and elders, at which an opportunity was given to hear the story, and says of the objectors that they rose up out of the crowd at a critical moment, being believers in Christ but still members of the sect of the Pharisees.

debates: Whether the objection of the Pharisees was raised at Antioch or at Jerusalem: Barnes reports the doubt and refers the verse to Jerusalem as Luke's own narrative, Calvin agrees and presses that the evil flowed from that fountain, while Clarke takes the verse as part of the report Paul and Barnabas made to the council about what had happened in Antioch

What the word rendered dissension implies: Barnes allows that it can mean sedition or intestine war but confines it here to earnest and warm discussion, while Calvin reads the episode as a contention grown hot enough that brethren fought as enemies
Whether this journey is the one Paul describes as made by revelation: Wesley harmonises the two by making the church's sending itself the vehicle of the revelation

What being brought on their way means: Gill leaves the choice open between escort and provision, Clarke takes it of provision and argues from the apostles' poverty, and Barnes takes it of escort as a Christian custom

Who received them at Jerusalem: Ellicott takes the words for a general gathering of members of different synagogues with their presiding elders, Calvin distinguishes the whole body from the apostles and elders who received them specially, and Robertson calls it simply a public reception
outliers: Ellicott's observation that the route through Samaria was chosen when Joppa would have avoided both the Canaanite cities and the hated Samaritans
Ellicott's note that this is the first distinct mention of any convert from the Pharisaic party, though the drift had begun in our Lord's ministry
Wesley's remark that even believers are apt to retain their former turn of mind and the prejudices derived from it
Calvin's inference from the appointment of companions that the whole church took the cause for its own
Clarke's argument that the church provided for the journey because the apostles had no property of their own
Robertson's picture of the objectors rising up out of the crowd at a critical moment
Calvin's note that the apostles had no certain place of abode at Jerusalem

6.pericope_label: The council assembled, and Peter rises to speak

schools.summary: Gill says the apostles and elders came together, and also the brethren or private members of the church, even the whole church, and that whether all the apostles were present is not certain, since Peter, James and John were, but who else cannot be said. Of the debate he says much was said pro and con upon the subject, many had spoken, and a great deal of time had been taken up about the thing in controversy. Calvin says Luke does not say that all the whole Church was gathered together, but those who excelled in doctrine and judgment and who, according to their office, were lawful judges in this matter; it may be that the disputation was had in the presence of the people, but no man should think otherwise of the assembly itself. Though there was choice made of grave men, and such as were public teachers of the Church, yet they could not agree at once, whereby it appears how the Lord exercised his Church even then; some were not so quick-witted that they could thoroughly see into the greatness of the matter, so that when they judged the law ought to be kept, being unadvisedly carried away with the zeal of the law, they did not see into how deep a labyrinth they threw the consciences of other men and their own also, thinking circumcision an eternal and inviolable token of God's covenant and holding the same opinion of the whole law. Peter therefore stands chiefly upon showing the state of the question, which most of them did not know, and his oration has two members: first he proves by the authority of God that the Gentiles must not be enforced to keep the law, and secondly he teaches that all man's salvation is overthrown if the conscience be once caught in this snare.

Henry says the council was called not by writ but by consent, and that the apostles and presbyters did not give their judgment separately but came together to hear one another's sense in the matter, since in the multitude of counsellors there is safety and satisfaction. They did not give their judgment rashly but considered the matter, and though clear in their own minds would take time to consider and to hear what might be said by the adverse party; nor did the apostles give their judgment without the elders, the inferior ministers, to whom they thus condescended and on whom they put an honour, for those that are most eminent in gifts and graces and in the most exalted stations in the church ought to show respect to their juniors and inferiors. Here, he says, is a direction to the pastors of the churches, when difficulties arise, to come together in solemn meetings for mutual advice and encouragement, that they may know one another's mind and strengthen one another's hands and act in concert. Of Peter he says he did not in the least pretend to any primacy or headship in this synod, and was not master of the assembly nor so much as chairman or moderator for the occasion; and from the words about purifying their hearts by faith he concludes that justification by faith and sanctification by the Holy Ghost cannot be separated, and that both are the gift of God. Lightfoot says that in the words a good while ago Peter had an eye to the saying of our Saviour, I will give thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that is, that he might first open the door of the gospel to the Gentiles; then it was that the Lord chose him, that by his mouth first the Gentiles might hear the word of the gospel and believe. This, Peter says, was done in former days, that is, in the time when Jesus went in and out among them, which the evangelists express as from the beginning.

Clarke says this was the first council ever held in the Christian Church, and that we find it was composed of the apostles and elders simply. The much disputing he attributes to those of the sect of the believing Pharisees, who strongly contended for circumcision, and reports the tradition that at the head of these was Cerinthus, a name famous in the primitive Church as one who laboured to unite the law and the Gospel. Wesley enters a qualification about the debate: it does not appear that this was among the apostles themselves, but if it had been, and if they themselves had debated at first, yet their final decision might be from an unerring direction, for however really they were inspired we need not suppose their inspiration was always so instantaneous as to preclude deliberation.

Barnes says they came together in accordance with the authority given in the Gospel, and that it would seem the whole church was convened on this occasion and concurred, at least, in the judgment expressed. Of the debate he objects to the English word: it is rather much inquiry or deliberation, since with our word disputing we commonly connect the idea of heat and anger, which is not necessarily implied in the word used here; it might have been calm, solemn, deliberate inquiry, and there is no evidence that it was conducted with undue heat. Ellicott says the meeting rightly takes its place as the first in the long series of councils, or synods, which mark the course of the Church's history, and that it bore its witness that the government of the Christian society was not to rest in the autocracy of a single will but in the deliberative decision of those who, directly or indirectly appointed by the choice or with the approval of the people, represented the whole community. Presbyters had an equal voice with the apostles, whose position was analogous to that of the later bishops, and those whom we should call the laity were present at the deliberations and gave their vote, though we have no absolute proof that they took part in them. Strictly speaking, in the later ecclesiastical language, it was a provincial and not an oecumenical synod, called to decide what seemed a question of discipline rather than of doctrine, but the ground on which the question had been argued made it one of world-wide dogmatic importance, since if circumcision was necessary then faith in Christ was insufficient, which Paul saw and felt in all its fulness and therefore would not give way by subjection, no, not for an hour. There are no data for estimating the number of presbyters present, though they probably included those of the neighbouring towns and villages of Judea. The much disputing implies to him a full discussion in which the Judaising teachers on one side and the advocates of freedom on the other took part; light is thrown on the character of the debate by Paul's own account, from which it appears that publicly he shrank from startling and offending the prejudices of his countrymen and was content to argue that circumcision and the Law were not binding upon the Gentiles, pressing the precedent of Cornelius and the analogy of the proselytes of the gate, while privately, in interviews with Peter, James and John, he had gone further and declared that for Jew and Gentile alike circumcision and the Law were hindrances and not helps to the spiritual life, and that faith working by love was everything; and they accepted his teaching, so that of all doctrines as to the development of the Christian Church, that which sees in Peter, James and John the leaders of a Judaising anti-Pauline party is perhaps the most baseless and fantastic. Peter's position, he adds, is one of authority but not of primacy, since he does not preside nor even propose a definite canon or resolution, his authority being that of personal and moral influence and nothing more; a good while ago is literally of ancient days, ten or twelve years having passed since the conversion of Cornelius, and we can hardly believe, as the Romish theory implies, that Peter came from the imperial city to attend the Council. Robertson notes that the church is not named here as it was at the earlier reception, but that we know from the verses following that the whole church came together this time also along with the apostles and elders, and that the Judaizers were evidently given full opportunity to air all their grievances and objections, being allowed plenty of time with no effort to shut off discussion.

debates: Who composed the council: Clarke and Calvin confine it to the apostles and elders as the lawful judges, Barnes, Gill and Robertson hold that the whole church was convened, and Ellicott goes further still and says the laity were present and gave their vote

Whether Peter presided: Henry says he did not pretend to any primacy or headship and was not so much as chairman, and Ellicott says his authority was personal and moral and nothing more, denying besides that he came from Rome to attend

How heated the debate was: Barnes objects that the English word imports heat and anger which the Greek need not carry, Robertson reads it as full and unhurried opportunity given to the objectors, and Calvin takes the disagreement itself as evidence that the Lord was exercising his Church

Whether the apostles themselves debated: Wesley doubts that they did, and adds that even if they had, their final decision might still be from an unerring direction, since inspiration need not be instantaneous

What kind of synod it was: Ellicott calls it strictly provincial rather than oecumenical and a question of discipline rather than doctrine, while holding that the ground of the argument made it of world-wide dogmatic importance
outliers: Ellicott's rule that the government of the Christian society was not to rest in the autocracy of a single will
Ellicott's judgement that the theory which makes Peter, James and John the leaders of a Judaising anti-Pauline party is the most baseless and fantastic of all
Ellicott's distinction between what Paul argued publicly at the council and what he had said privately to the three
Clarke's tradition that Cerinthus stood at the head of the believing Pharisees, labouring to unite the law and the Gospel
Lightfoot's reading of a good while ago as an allusion to the promise of the keys, given that Peter might first open the door of the gospel to the Gentiles
Calvin's warning that zeal for the law threw consciences into a deep labyrinth without those who felt it perceiving as much
Henry's direction that pastors should meet in solemn assembly when difficulties arise, and that the eminent should honour their juniors

8.pericope_label: Peter on the witness of the Spirit and the unbearable yoke

schools.summary: Gill says God, being omniscient, the searcher of the hearts and the trier of the reins of the children of men, knew with what sincerity Cornelius sent for Peter and with what vehement desire and longing expectation he and his family and friends waited for his coming. He puts no difference between us and them either in the extraordinary gifts or in the special grace of the Spirit, giving them the same graces of faith, hope and love, admitting them to the same privileges and immunities of the house of God, and giving them a right and title to the same inheritance. To tempt God he takes of hesitating about the matter, disputing upon the point and seeking further proof and evidence of the will of God in the affair, when it is so plain a case that it has been his will the Gospel should be preached to the Gentiles without obliging them to circumcision. Calvin enters a qualification against the plain statement: there was indeed some difference, because the Gentiles who were uncircumcised were suddenly admitted unto the covenant of eternal life, whereas the Jews were prepared by circumcision unto faith; but Peter's meaning is that they were both alike chosen. The second part of the sermon he takes to show how deadly the doctrine was which Paul's enemies sought to bring in, since it might drown godly souls in despair: God is tempted if the Gentiles be forced to keep the law of necessity, for the Gentiles would have injury done them if more were required at their hands than God will, and seeing he made them equal with the holy people and vouchsafed them the honour of adoption it was an absurd matter that they should be rejected and his liberality restrained; this faith is sufficient for them, though they want ceremonies. Then Peter takes a higher principle, that those who tie men's salvation to the works of the law leave them no good hope but rather throw the whole world headlong into horrible destruction, if it can obtain salvation by no other means than by keeping the law. As touching the words, since Scripture says that God is tempted divers ways, Peter's meaning here is that God is provoked as it were of set purpose when a heavier burden is laid upon men than they are able to bear.

Clarke notes that the epithet for the God who knows the hearts occurs nowhere else in the New Testament than here and at the choosing of Matthias, and takes God's bearing them witness to mean that he considered them proper or fit to receive the Gospel of Christ. Giving the Holy Spirit to the uncircumcised just as he had given it to the circumcised he calls an evident proof that, in the judgment of God, circumcision was no preparation to receive the Gospel of Christ. On tempting God he asks why, when God by giving the Holy Spirit to the Gentiles evidently shows that he does not design them to be circumcised in order to become debtors to the law, men will provoke him to displeasure by doing what he evidently designs shall not be done. The yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear he refers not to the moral law, which was of eternal obligation, but to the ritual law, which through the multitude of its sacrifices and ordinances was exceedingly burdensome to the Jewish people; had not God by an especial providence rendered both their fields and their flocks very fruitful, they could not possibly have borne so painful a ritual. He retails besides a rabbinic story in which Korah is represented as showing the oppressive nature of the law and the avarice of its priests in justification of his rebellion, the widow with two orphan children being forbidden to plough with an ox and an ass together, to sow her field with divers seeds, and to reap the corners and the gleanings that belonged to the poor. Wesley says God bore them witness in that he accepted them by giving them the Holy Ghost, that purifying is a word repeated from the account of Cornelius, that the heart is the proper seat of purity and faith the means, without concerning themselves with the Mosaic law, and asks in a line why they provoke God to anger by putting so heavy a yoke on the disciples' neck.

Barnes says God knew whether they were true converts or not and gave a demonstration that he acknowledged them as his, and that though they had not been circumcised and did not conform to the law of Moses he put no difference, showing that the observance of these rites was not necessary in order to the true conversion of men and to acceptance with him, and that he gave the Jews no advantage. To tempt God he takes as provoking him to displeasure: since he has shown his determination to accept them without such rites, to attempt to impose them on his own people without his authority and against his manifest will is to provoke him, the argument being that God had already accepted them. Ellicott notes the recurrence of the epithet for the heart-knowing God as characteristic of Peter, and says that the denial of any difference obviously implies the most entire acceptance of the teaching which Paul had privately communicated to the three who were as the pillars of the Church, the very words of Peter being almost reproduced in the Epistle to the Romans. To tempt God, he says, was to make the experiment whether his will, manifested in the acceptance of the Gentiles, or man's will, resenting and resisting it, was the stronger of the two, and nothing but defeat and condemnation could be the issue of such a trial. Of the yoke he says no words of Paul's in relation to the Law could be stronger or clearer than these; they reproduced our Lord's own language as to the heavy burdens of the Pharisaic traditions and his own easy yoke, and were echoed by Paul when he warned the Galatians not to be entangled again in the yoke of bondage, while the words that follow speak out the experience of the Apostle himself in terms hardly less striking than those of Paul in the seventh of Romans, though they deal with the Law in its positive rather than its prohibitive aspect. Robertson calls the epithet a late word found in the New Testament only here and at the choosing of Matthias, notes that the Spirit was given before their baptism and that this was the Lord's doing, and says that in the matter of faith and conversion God treated Jews as heathen and heathen as Jews, distinguishing nothing between them. Tempting God he explains as implying that God had made a mistake this time, though right about Cornelius, and calls it a home-thrust: they were refusing to follow the guidance of God as the Israelites did at Massah and Meribah.

debates: Whether there was truly no difference between Jew and Gentile: Calvin insists there was some, since the Gentiles were suddenly admitted while the Jews had been prepared by circumcision unto faith, and confines Peter's meaning to the equality of their election, while the others take the denial at full strength

What tempting God means here: Ellicott makes it an experiment whether God's will or man's is the stronger, Robertson an insinuation that God had erred this time though right about Cornelius, Barnes a provocation by imposing rites without authority, Gill a hesitation where the case is already plain, and Calvin the laying on of a burden heavier than men can bear

Which law the unbearable yoke refers to: Clarke excludes the moral law as of eternal obligation and confines it to the ritual law, arguing that only a special providence over fields and flocks made so painful a ritual bearable at all

How far Peter's argument reaches: Calvin says he rises past the injury done the Gentiles to the fountain itself, that tying salvation to works of law leaves no good hope and throws the world headlong into destruction
Whether the Spirit preceded baptism in the case of Cornelius: Robertson states plainly that it did, and that this was the Lord's doing
outliers: Clarke's rabbinic story of Korah justifying his rebellion by the law's oppressiveness towards a widow with two orphan children
Ellicott's judgement that no words of Paul's about the Law are stronger or clearer than these words of Peter's
Robertson's reversal, that in faith and conversion God treated Jews as heathen and heathen as Jews
Robertson's comparison of the council's hesitation with Israel at Massah and Meribah
Ellicott's observation that Romans reproduces almost the very words of Peter here
Calvin's concession that a real difference existed even while the equality was affirmed
Clarke's note that the epithet for the heart-knowing God occurs only twice in the New Testament, both times on Peter's lips

11.pericope_label: The grace of the Lord Jesus, the silence of the assembly, and James rising last

schools.summary: Gill notes that those who believe here are the circumcised, and that what follows is a sure and certain article of faith. Of the silence he says that upon Peter's oration there was a profound silence in the whole assembly, among all the brethren of the church who had come together on the occasion, who were satisfied and acquiesced by their silence. On the name Simeon he says James begins by taking notice of Peter's speech and agrees to it and confirms it, and that by Simeon is not meant, as some have thought, the Simeon who took Christ in his arms, who had been dead long ago, but Simon Peter. Calvin compares the two things Peter sets against each other as contraries, to have hope of salvation in the grace of Christ and to be under the yoke of the law, a comparison which greatly sets out the justification that comes by Christ. Of the silence he says Luke gives us to understand that the Spirit of God so reigned in that assembly that they yielded forthwith to reason: the disputation was hot before, but now, after Peter has laid open the counsel of God and handled the question, it ceases. On the identity of James he reports that some old writers of the Church think this James was one of the disciples, surnamed Justus and Oblias, whose cruel death is recorded by Josephus in the twentieth book of his Antiquities, and wishes the old writers had travailed rather to know the man than to set him forth with feigned ornament.

Clarke reads the closing sentence as an answer to an objection, whether God had not designed to save the Jews by an observance of the law and the Gentiles by the faith of the Gospel, and answers that the Jews can be saved only as the Gentiles are. He analyses Peter's speech in numbered steps, that circumcision is a sign of the purification of the heart, that this purification can only be effected by the Holy Ghost, and that the Holy Ghost had been given to the uncircumcised, and says the strong facts stated could not be controverted, which is why all the multitude kept silence. Of James he says he was evidently president of the council and is generally called bishop of Jerusalem: the rest either argued on the subject or gave their opinion, but James alone pronounced the definitive sentence, which he would not have done had Peter been prince and head of the apostles and of the Church. He returns to the point at the next verse, remarking that James does not give Peter even the title he received from our Lord at the time when he is supposed to have been made head of the Church and vicar of Christ upon earth, so that it is evident James did not understand our Lord as giving Peter any such office. Wesley notes that Peter does not say our Lord, because in this solemn place he means the Lord of all, and that we Jews shall be saved even as they, the Gentiles, namely through the grace of the Lord Jesus and not by our observance of the ceremonial law; that the miracles and wonders reported confirmed what Peter had said; and that James, the apostle of the Hebrews, calls Peter by his Hebrew name, taking a people for his name to mean a people who believe in him and are called by his name.

Barnes says the apostles who speak are those who had been with the Gentiles and had seen the evidences of their acceptance with God, and that salvation is by the grace or mercy of Christ alone, without any of the rites and ceremonies of the Jews. The multitude that kept silence he takes for the multitude of private Christians assembled on the occasion, and argues that it does not refer to a synod of ministers and elders merely, since the church and the brethren are represented as having been present. Of James he says this was James the Less, the son of Alpheus, and that the whole transaction shows Peter had no such authority in the church as the Papists pretend, since otherwise his opinion would have been followed without debate, James having an authority not less than that of Peter. Simeon he calls a Hebrew name of which the common Greek form was Simon, and one of the names of Peter, and to take out of them a people he explains as choosing from among the Gentiles those who should be God's friends. Ellicott treats the closing sentence as the last argument in a summary of Peter's speech, since the Pharisee might regard the Law as binding, but even he, if he believed in Christ, was compelled to confess where his hope lay. The leaders of the Church, he says, had clearly reserved their part in the debate to the last, the two apostles of the Gentiles being now called on to repeat more publicly what they had already narrated to the apostles and elders. The position of James in the Council he calls clearly one of pre-eminence, justifying the title of Bishop of Jerusalem which later writers give him, since no one speaks after him and he sums up the whole. On the name he notes that the Greek form is Symeon, as in the Second Epistle of Peter, and that the use of the old Hebrew form instead of the more familiar Simon was natural in a Galilean speaker and is presumptive evidence in favour of our having a report from notes made at the time. Robertson renders the clause more exactly as our believing that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus in like manner as they also, and calls the note thoroughly Pauline. The silence he takes as an ingressive aorist, all the multitude becoming silent after Peter's speech and because of it, the imperfect that follows being descriptive of their rapt attention. Of James he says he was termed James the Just and was considered a representative of the Hebraic as opposed to the Hellenistic wing of the Jewish Christians, so that the Judaizers had doubtless counted on him as a champion of their view.

Chrysostom says this James was bishop, as they say, and therefore he speaks last, and herein is fulfilled the saying that in the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established. He bids us observe the discretion shown by James also, in making his argument good from the prophets rather than from his own authority.

debates: Which James presided: Barnes takes him for James the Less, the son of Alpheus, Ellicott for James the brother of the Lord, and Calvin reports the old writers who make him the disciple surnamed Justus and Oblias whose death Josephus records, while wishing they had troubled to know the man instead of embellishing him

What James's speaking last proves: Chrysostom infers that he was bishop, Clarke that he was president of the council and alone pronounced the definitive sentence, Ellicott that his position was one of pre-eminence, and Barnes that Peter can have had no such authority as is claimed for him, since otherwise his opinion would have been followed without debate

Who the multitude that kept silence were: Barnes argues expressly that they were private Christians and not a synod of ministers and elders, since the church and the brethren are represented as present

Whom Simeon denotes: Gill rules out the aged man who took Christ in his arms, long since dead, and takes it of Simon Peter, while Ellicott makes the archaic form itself evidence that the speech was reported from notes taken at the time

What the closing sentence answers: Clarke takes it as a reply to the supposition that Jews are saved by law and Gentiles by faith, while Calvin makes it a contrast of contraries between the grace of Christ and the yoke of the law
outliers: Ellicott's argument that the Hebrew form Symeon is presumptive evidence for a report taken down at the time
Calvin's complaint that the old writers embellished James instead of troubling to identify him
Robertson's note that the Judaizers had counted on James as a champion of their view
Clarke's observation that James does not accord Peter the title he had received from our Lord
Calvin's reading of the silence as evidence that the Spirit so reigned in the assembly that they yielded forthwith to reason
Wesley's remark that Peter says the Lord Jesus and not our Lord because in this solemn place he means the Lord of all
Chrysostom's application of the rule of two or three witnesses to the order of the speeches

15.pericope_label: The prophecy of Amos and the sentence of James

schools.summary: Gill says several of the prophecies of the Old Testament plainly speak of the calling of the Gentiles, though James thought it sufficient to produce only one instead of many. The promise to return he refers to the time after the Lord had destroyed the sinful kingdom from off the face of the earth and sifted the house of Israel among all nations, after which he promises to return and show favour. That the residue of men might seek after the Lord he explains of attending his worship, praying to him, and seeking to him for life and salvation, the same being called in Amos the remnant. The words about God's works known from the beginning he says are the words of James and not of Amos: all the things which God does in the church and in the world were foreknown and predetermined by him from the beginning of the world, or from eternity. Of the closing formula he says James gave his opinion or judgment in the case, what he reckoned most advisable to be done, and did not impose his sense upon the whole body but proposed it to them. Calvin says we see how the apostles took nothing to themselves imperiously but reverently followed what was prescribed in the word of God, and that it did not grieve them nor did they count it any disgrace to profess themselves the scholars of the Scripture. Because the place is not cited word for word as it stands in the prophet, he says, we must see what difference there is, though it is not necessary to examine straitly what diversity there is in the words, so long as it appears that the prophecy fitly agrees with the matter in hand. The clause about seeking he takes as added by James by way of exposition, not found or read in the prophet and yet not superfluous, since to be numbered among the people of God we must on our side seek him. The sentence about God's works he calls a prevention or anticipation, put in to remove the hatred which might have arisen upon the novelty, since the sudden change might have been suspected and therefore troubled weak minds. On the closing judgment he notes that James denies the Gentiles must be driven from the Church through disagreement about ceremonies, seeing they were admitted by God, yet seems contrary to himself when he denies they ought to be troubled and yet prescribes certain things.

Lightfoot argues from the language of the speech itself, holding that it will hardly be denied by any that James spoke now in Hebrew, that is, in the Syriac tongue, and drawing consequences from that for the form of the citation. On the fallen tabernacle of David he brings a rabbinic exchange in which Rab Nachman asks R. Isaac whence he is taught when the son of the fallen will come, the title being derived from the very words of Amos about the tabernacle of David which is fallen down, so that the Jewish schools themselves read the passage of the Messiah.

Clarke says Peter had asserted the fact of the conversion of the Gentiles and James shows that fact to be the fulfilment of declarations made by the prophets. The two verses of the citation, he says, are quoted from Amos nearly as they now stand in the best editions of the Septuagint and are evidently taken from that version, which differs considerably from the Hebrew text; where the Hebrew has that they may possess the remnant of Edom, it is evident that in the copy which the Seventy translated they found a verb meaning that they might seek instead of one meaning that they might possess. The words about God's works known from the beginning he takes to mean that this is not a new counsel of God, who had purposed from the time he called the Israelites to make the Gentiles partakers of the same grace and mercy. Of the closing formula he says there is an authority here that does not appear in the speech of Peter, that this authority was felt and bowed to by all the council, and that the decree proposed by James was adopted. Wesley says Peter had urged the plain fact which James confirms by Scripture prophecy, one prophet being immediately cited. After this he glosses as after the Jewish dispensation expires, and the building again of the fallen tabernacle of David as the raising from David's seed of the Christ, who shall build on the ruins of that fallen tabernacle a spiritual and eternal kingdom. The Gentiles on whom God's name is called he explains as those who are called by his name and are his people; and the knowledge of all God's works from eternity he infers from the prophecy itself and its accomplishment, so that the conversion of the Gentiles, being known to God from eternity, ought not to be thought a new or strange thing.

Barnes says it was a very material point with them, as Jews, to inquire whether this was in accordance with the predictions of the Scriptures. The quotation, he says, is not made literally either from the Hebrew or the Septuagint, which itself differs from the Hebrew: the seventeenth verse is quoted literally from the Septuagint, but in the sixteenth the general sense only of the passage is retained. The phrase the residue of men he takes to be understood both by the Seventy and by James as referring to others than Jews. The sentence about God's works he explains to mean that God sees everything future, knows what he will accomplish, has a plan, and so arranges all his works in his mind that he sees them distinctly. Of the closing formula he notes that the Greek means I judge, the usual language in which a judge delivers his opinion, but that it does not imply that James assumed authority to settle the case, merely that he gave his opinion or counsel. Ellicott notes the mode of quoting without naming the prophet, and finds it a fact not without interest that the prophet from whom the words are taken had already been quoted by Stephen, so that those who listened may have been led to turn to his writings. The Hebrew, he says, gives that they may possess the remnant of Edom and of all the heathen which are called by my name, and the Septuagint translators either paraphrased the passage so as to give a wider and more general meaning or read a different text. The clause about God's works he says the better manuscripts give in the singular, his work, that is, the great work of the government and education of mankind, and the words are an implicit answer to the charge of innovation, since if the work were of God it could not be so called. The closing formula he takes as the tone of one who speaks with authority, though what follows is given not as a decree but as a resolution submitted to the judgment of the apostles and elders. Robertson notes that James cites only Amos, and from the Septuagint, that the verb for building again is a compound of the verb used by Jesus of the church, and that the tabernacle of David is a poetical figure of the throne of David; the words about the beginning he takes as added by James, perhaps with a reminiscence of Isaiah, the point being that this purpose of God is an old one and that God has an Israel outside of and beyond the old one. The closing formula he calls a summing up of the case by the President of the Conference.

debates: How far the citation departs from the Hebrew and why: Barnes distinguishes the verse quoted literally from the Greek from the one that keeps only the general sense, Clarke explains the divergence by a variant verb in the copy the Seventy translated, Ellicott leaves paraphrase and variant reading as open alternatives, and Calvin declines to examine the words closely so long as the prophecy fits the matter in hand

How much authority James claims in his closing formula: Gill says he proposed rather than imposed and Barnes that the words do not imply he assumed authority to settle the case, while Clarke says the authority is one that does not appear in Peter's speech and was bowed to by the whole council, Robertson calls him President of the Conference, and Ellicott allows the tone of authority while denying that a decree was issued

Whose words the sentence about God's works are: Gill and Robertson agree that James adds them and that they are not from Amos, Robertson hearing a reminiscence of Isaiah, while Calvin treats the addition as a deliberate anticipation of the charge of novelty
In what language James spoke: Lightfoot holds it will hardly be denied that he spoke in Hebrew, that is in the Syriac tongue, which bears directly on the form in which the prophecy is cited
Whether James contradicts himself: Calvin raises the objection that he denies the Gentiles ought to be troubled and then prescribes certain things
outliers: Lightfoot's rabbinic exchange in which the Messiah is asked after under the title of the son of the fallen, drawn from the fallen tabernacle of David
Clarke's textual conjecture that the Seventy read a verb meaning to seek where the Hebrew has one meaning to possess
Ellicott's note that the better manuscripts read God's work in the singular, the great work of the government and education of mankind
Ellicott's observation that Amos had already been quoted by Stephen, so that his hearers may have been led to the prophet's writings
Calvin's principle that exact verbal agreement in a citation matters less than the fitness of the prophecy to the matter in hand
Robertson's remark that God has an Israel outside of and beyond the old one
Gill's note that James produced one prophecy where many were available

20.pericope_label: The four things enjoined, and the reason drawn from Moses

schools.summary: Gill says the direction is to send an epistle to the Gentiles to this effect, concerning the following things, and on the closing verse that for many years past, even from the times of Ezra, the law of Moses had been publicly expounded by those whom the Jews call preachers or expounders in every city where there were synagogues. Calvin says there appears a manifest reason why particular commandment was given concerning things offered to idols, blood, and that which was strangled: they were of themselves things indifferent, yet such as had some special thing in them more than other rites of the law, since we know how straitly the Lord commands us to eschew those things which are contrary to the external profession of faith. Of the closing verse he says the place has in his judgment been badly expounded and drawn into a contrary sense, since interpreters think James adds it because it were superfluous to prescribe anything to the Jews, who were well acquainted with the doctrine of the law and to whom it was read every Sabbath, and so pick out the meaning that they should be content to require these few things of the Gentiles, who were not accustomed to bear the yoke of the law, while the Jews had Moses out of whom they might learn more. Some also gather from the place that circumcision with its appurtenances ought to be observed even at this day among the Jews, but they reason unfitly and unskilfully, even if the exposition he has set down were true. James had a far other meaning: he teaches that ceremonies cannot be abolished so quickly, as it were at the first dash, because the Jews had now a long time been acquainted with the doctrine of the law and Moses had his preachers, and therefore it stood them upon to redeem concord for a short time, until such time as the liberty gotten by Christ might by little and little appear more plainly. This is what the common proverb says, that it was meet the old ceremonies should be buried with some honour.

Lightfoot asks with good reason whether these four things were forbidden under one and the same notion, namely that the converted Gentiles might not give offence to the Jews if they should not abstain from all of them, or whether there might not be something else interwoven, namely that those converted Gentiles might not relapse into something of their former heathenism; the abstaining from pollutions of idols and from fornication seems to him to respect the latter, as the abstaining from things strangled and from blood respects the former. He wonders meanwhile at the heart and forehead of the Nicolaitans, who not only practised but taught diametrically contrary to this decree of the apostles, and asks with what paint those Balaamites and Jezebelites could beautify their horrid doctrine and practice, whether it was the liberty of the gospel they pretended, or whether they did not rather abuse the love and charity commanded in the gospel, making a show of some more transcendent friendship among themselves.

Clarke enumerates the four things prohibited in the decree, pollutions of idols, fornication, things strangled and blood, and says that by the first, or as it stands later meats offered to idols, not only was all idolatry forbidden but the eating of things offered in sacrifice to idols knowing that they were thus offered, and the joining with idolaters in their sacred feasts. Of the closing verse he says the sense seems to be that as it was necessary to write to the Gentiles what was strictly necessary for them to observe relative to these points, it was not so to the converted Jews, for they had Moses. Wesley says the abstinence from fornication is enjoined against a sin which even the philosophers among the heathens did not account any fault, and which was particularly frequent in the worship of their idols, on which account the two are here named together; things strangled he explains as whatever had been killed without pouring out the blood, and refers the prohibition back to the command given to Noah and in him to all his posterity. Of the closing verse he suggests that perhaps the connection is that to the Jews we need write nothing on these heads, for they hear the law continually.

Barnes says the verse has greatly perplexed commentators, the main grounds of difficulty being why fornication, an offence against the moral law about which there could be no dispute, should have been included, and whether the prohibition to abstain from blood is still binding. The pollutions of idols he takes evidently of the flesh of animals offered in sacrifice, which after being offered was often exposed for sale in the markets or served up at feasts, so that whether it was right for Christians to partake became a very important question, the Jews contending that it was in fact partaking of idolatry and the Gentile converts alleging that they did not eat it as a sacrifice; to partake might not be morally wrong, but it would give occasion for scandal and offence, and therefore as a matter of expediency abstinence was advised. The word rendered fornication he says is applicable to all illicit intercourse. Of the closing verse he says the meaning is that the law of Moses prohibiting these things was read in the synagogues constantly, and that as the Jewish converts would not soon learn that their ceremonial law had ceased to be binding, the Gentiles should avoid what would offend them. Ellicott says the grounds of the measure are not far to seek: it was of the nature of a compromise, since the Gentiles could not complain that the burden imposed was very grievous, and the Pharisee section of the Church could not refuse admission to those who fulfilled these conditions when they had admitted the proselytes of the gate on like conditions to their synagogues; and the rules found a place among the seven precepts traditionally ascribed to Noah, which were held binding upon all mankind while the Law as such was binding on Israel only, and had therefore been thought sufficient for the proselytes of the gate. The first noun he says is found only in the Septuagint and the New Testament, its primary idea perhaps being that of wallowing in blood and mire and so incurring pollution; as distinguished from the acts that follow it indicates any participation, publicly or privately, in idolatrous rites, so that one who acted on the rule would have to refrain from entering a temple and to dislodge busts or statues of the gods from his house and gardens, the presence of such things being a great stumbling-block to devout Jews, and the Gentile convert who might have kept them as works of art being required to renounce them, the statues of Zeus and Artemis and Hermes being henceforth to him as abominations. Under the religion of Greece and Rome, he adds, sacrifices were so common that it might fairly be taken for granted that the flesh at any festive meal had been offered, a small portion being burnt on the altar and the rest cooked for the household or sent to market. Of the closing verse he says the conjunction gives the reason for writing to the Gentiles and giving them these injunctions, since the Jews, who heard the Law in their synagogues every Sabbath, did not need instruction. Robertson notes that the verb for writing is the one from which our word epistle comes, and that the mention of Moses gives a reason why these four necessary things are named, since in every city there are synagogues where rabbis proclaim these matters, so that Gentile Christians would be giving constant offence to neglect them.

debates: On what ground the four things were forbidden: Lightfoot divides them, referring the pollutions of idols and fornication to the danger of relapse into heathenism and things strangled and blood to the danger of offending Jews, while Barnes makes the whole a matter of expediency and Calvin holds the food rules to be indifferent in themselves yet bound up with the external profession of faith

Why fornication stands among ceremonial rules: Barnes reports that commentators have been greatly perplexed by the inclusion of a moral offence about which there could be no dispute, and Wesley answers from heathen opinion, that the philosophers did not account it a fault and that it belonged to idol worship

What pollutions of idols covers: Ellicott extends it to any participation in idolatrous rites, including the keeping of statues as works of art, while Barnes and Clarke confine it to sacrificial meat and the sharing of idolatrous feasts

What the closing verse about Moses is for: Ellicott, Clarke, Wesley, Barnes and Gill all take it as the reason for writing to the Gentiles and not to the Jews, who hear the law weekly, Robertson turns it into the reason why these four things are named at all, and Calvin says the place has been badly expounded and drawn into a contrary sense
Whether the passage supports the continuance of circumcision among Jews: Calvin reports that some gather this from the verse and answers that they reason unfitly and unskilfully
outliers: Ellicott's derivation of the four rules from the seven precepts traditionally ascribed to Noah, binding on all mankind while the Law bound Israel only
Ellicott's picture of the convert required to dislodge the statues of Zeus, Artemis and Hermes from his house and gardens
Calvin's proverb that it was meet the old ceremonies should be buried with some honour
Lightfoot's attack on the Nicolaitans, who taught as well as practised the contrary of this decree
Wesley's derivation of the rule against things strangled from the command given to Noah and in him to all his posterity
Gill's tracing of the synagogue exposition of the law back to the times of Ezra
Ellicott's remark that under Greek and Roman religion it might fairly be assumed that the flesh at any festive meal had been sacrificed

22.pericope_label: The decision of the whole church and the letter it sends

schools.summary: Gill says the opinion, judgment and advice of James was approved by the whole body of apostles, ministers and brethren of the church assembled on the occasion, and that they agreed unanimously. Of the letter he notes that the messengers were not made use of as amanuenses to write it for them, but that being written it was put into their hands and sent by them; and of the opening words that the report had come by Paul and Barnabas, who were sent by the church at Antioch to Jerusalem to acquaint them with the state of their case. Calvin says that tempest was made calm not without the singular grace of God, so that after the matter had been thoroughly discussed they did all agree together in sound doctrine, and that the modesty of the common people may be gathered from this, since they referred the matter to the judgment of others. On the mention of the troublers he says we see that there was no respect of persons among these holy men, which always corrupts sound and right judgments: they confess that there were knaves of their own company, and yet they do not in any way flatter them or, through corrupt favour, incline towards them.

Henry says we have here the result of the consultation held at Jerusalem about the imposing of the ceremonial law upon the Gentiles, that much more was likely said about it than is recorded, but that at length it was brought to a head and the advice which James gave was universally approved and agreed to.

Clarke divides the parts taken in the decision, that James determined what ought to be done and the whole assembly resolved how that should be done, and notes that Paul and Barnabas were to return and could have witnessed to the church at Antioch what had been decided. Of the letter he says there was no occasion to send such an epistle to the brethren which were of the Jews, because the law which had been so long read in their synagogues taught them all those things, and therefore the epistle is sent exclusively to the Gentiles. Of the troublers he observes that the persons who produced these doubtful disputations at Antioch had gone out from the apostles at Jerusalem and were of that Church, persons zealous for the law and yet, strange to tell, so conscientious in that zeal. Wesley notes that the whole Church therefore had a part in the decision, and that chosen men were sent who might put it beyond all dispute that this was the judgment of the apostles and all the brethren. The whole conduct of this affair, he says, plainly shows that the Church in those days had no conception of Peter's primacy, or of his being the chief judge in controversies, for the decree is drawn up not according to his proposal but according to that of the apostle James. Of the letter itself he remarks that its simplicity, weightiness and conciseness are highly observable.

Barnes says it seemed fit and proper to the apostles and elders, to whom the business had been particularly referred, and to the whole church, all the Christians there assembled, who concurred in the sentiment and expressed it. Of the letter he notes that the Greek is having written and does not mean that they wrote more than one epistle, that it was sent by their hand, and that the greeting is a word of salutation expressing their desire for the happiness of the persons addressed. The complaint against the troublers he glosses as troubling them with doctrines, disturbing their minds and producing contentions, and observes that the word rendered subverting your souls occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Ellicott says the words about the whole church are important as showing the position occupied by the laity: if they concurred in the letter it must have been submitted to their approval, and the right to approve involves the power to reject and probably to amend. What follows, he says, unless we assume a deliberate fraud, is clearly the transcript of a document, the first in the long list of decrees and canons and encyclical letters which mark the Church's history. The reference to those who went out is obviously to the teachers who had appeared at Antioch, whose names are wisely and charitably suppressed. Robertson notes that the opening of the decree is a regular idiom, that this irenicon of James commended itself to the whole assembly, and that apparently a vote was taken which was unanimous, the Judaizers probably not voting. Of the letter he observes the anacoluthon in the participle, and that the committee of four, Judas, Silas, Barnabas and Paul, carried it. The mention of those who went out from us he calls a direct blow at the Judaizers, put in delicate language, since it speaks as if the trouble had arisen only at Antioch and not also in Jerusalem in open meeting.

debates: What part the laity had in the decision: Ellicott says the words about the whole church show that the letter must have been submitted to their approval, and that the right to approve involves the power to reject, while Wesley infers simply that they had a part, Clarke divides determining from resolving, and Calvin reads the same fact as evidence of the common people's modesty in referring the matter to others

Whose proposal the decree follows: Wesley makes the drafting itself an argument that the Church of that day had no conception of Peter's primacy, since the decree is drawn according to the proposal of James
What the document before us is: Ellicott holds that, short of assuming deliberate fraud, it is the transcript of an actual letter and the first of the Church's decrees and encyclicals

How far the troublers are censured: Calvin praises the refusal to flatter knaves of their own company, Ellicott notes the charitable suppression of their names, and Robertson finds the language delicate to the point of speaking as though the trouble had been only at Antioch
To whom the letter was addressed and why: Clarke argues that no such letter was needed for Jewish believers, since the law read in their synagogues already taught them these things
outliers: Ellicott's argument that the right to approve the letter involves the power to reject and probably to amend it
Ellicott's description of the letter as the first in the long list of decrees, canons and encyclical letters that mark the Church's history
Robertson's supposition that a unanimous vote was taken with the Judaizers abstaining
Robertson's calling the proposal of James an irenicon
Clarke's observation that the troublers had gone out from the apostles at Jerusalem and were of that very church
Barnes's note that the word rendered subverting your souls occurs nowhere else in the New Testament
Wesley's judgement on the letter's simplicity, weightiness and conciseness

25.pericope_label: The letter delivered, and the Spirit joined to the decree

schools.summary: Gill says the assembly was in one place and also in one mind, and that they had reason from various things to conclude that they were under the influence and direction of the Holy Ghost in the affair, among them the spirit of prayer that was among them and the power that attended their deliberation. The hazarding of their lives he illustrates from Antioch in Pisidia, where a persecution was raised against them and they were expelled out of the coasts of that place, and from Lystra, where Paul was stoned and left for dead. The abstaining from meats offered to idols he says explains what was meant by pollutions of idols, and of the dismissal he notes that Paul and Barnabas with Judas and Silas were dismissed by the apostles, elders and church at Jerusalem. Calvin says the praises given to Paul and Barnabas are set against the slanders by which the false apostles had essayed to bring them out of credit. Where the apostles and elders match and join themselves with the Holy Ghost, he says, they attribute nothing to themselves apart, the speech importing as much as if they had said that the Holy Ghost was the captain, guide and governor and that they followed. Of the reading of the letter he says it was the most lawful kind of dealing to admit the whole multitude to it, for if any controversy falls out in the doctrine of faith it is meet that the judgment be referred over to the learned and the godly.

Clarke calls the description of Paul and Barnabas a high character, since they had already suffered much in the cause of Christ and exposed their lives to the most imminent danger, and were intent on the same service still. Judas and Silas he takes as proofs that the testimony of Paul and Barnabas was true and that the letter was not forged, since they could witness by word of mouth to the same things the letter contained. Of the claim to the Spirit he says the whole council had met under his direction, had consulted under his influence, and gave forth their decree from his especial inspiration; and the necessary things he says were necessary howsoever burdensome they might seem. If the Gentiles did not keep themselves from these things, he adds, they would do ill, that is, they would sin against God whose Spirit had commanded them to keep from them, and no one can do any of these forbidden things and keep a guiltless conscience. Wesley notes that the words about hazarding their lives are spoken of Paul and Barnabas, and on the decree that all these things were necessary for that time, but that the first of them was not necessary long, the direction concerning it being therefore repealed by the same Spirit, as we read in the former Epistle to the Corinthians. On blood he argues that the eating of it was never permitted the children of God from the beginning of the world, since from Adam to Noah no man ate flesh at all and consequently no man then ate blood, and when God allowed Noah and his posterity to eat flesh he expressly forbade the blood.

Barnes calls the description of Paul and Barnabas a noble testimony to their character, a commendation of them to the confidence of the churches and an implied expression of trust. Of Judas and Silas he says they would confirm by their own statements the same things that had been written. The claim that it seemed good to the Holy Ghost he calls a strong and undoubted claim to inspiration, noting that it was with special reference to the organisation of the church that the Holy Spirit had been promised by the Lord Jesus. The abstaining from meats offered to idols he says explains what is meant by pollutions of idols, and the closing commendation means that they will do what ought to be done in regard to the subjects of dispute. Ellicott renders the opening literally, being of one mind, unanimously, and to choose men and send them unto you, and identifies the men as Barsabas and Silas. From the words about hazarding their lives he infers that the narrative of the hairbreadth escapes at the Pisidian Antioch and at Lystra must have been laid before the Church. Of the claim to the Spirit he says the measure was, as the apostles were persuaded, one of wisdom and charity, and they could not ascribe those gifts to any other source than the Spirit who gives a right judgment in all things. The specific term for meats offered to idols, he notes, takes the place of the more general word James had used, and the change, if the two words were not used as altogether equivalent, may be thought of as favouring the Gentiles by narrowing the prohibition. Of the return he thinks it natural, in the absence of anything to the contrary, to infer that they went back as they had come, through Samaria and Phoenicia, gladdening the hearts of the disciples there by telling them of the result. Robertson notes that the formula of decision recurs three times in the chapter and that this definite decision is now in the epistle itself, renders the participle of hazarding as having handed over their lives to another, and calls the mention of the Spirit a definite claim that the church in this action had his guidance, a fact plain to them from what had taken place. The adverb rendered necessary he calls an old one occurring only here in the New Testament, and observes that in comparison with the freedom won this burden is light. Of the dismissal he supposes religious services may have been held and perhaps an escort given.

debates: Whether the necessary things were permanently binding: Wesley says all were necessary for that time but that the first was repealed by the same Spirit, as the Corinthian Epistle shows, while Clarke insists they were necessary however burdensome and that failure to keep them would be sin against the Spirit who commanded them

What the joining of the Holy Ghost to the decree claims: Barnes calls it a strong and undoubted claim to inspiration and Robertson a definite claim to guidance, Clarke traces the whole council's deliberation to the Spirit's influence, Ellicott infers the Spirit from the wisdom and charity of the measure itself, and Calvin insists the apostles attribute nothing to themselves apart, the Spirit being captain and guide

Why the letter substitutes meats offered to idols for pollutions of idols: Ellicott alone raises it and suggests the change may favour the Gentiles by narrowing the prohibition, while Gill and Barnes treat the later phrase as simply explaining the earlier

Why the letter commends its own bearers: Calvin makes the praises a direct answer to the slanders of the false apostles, while Barnes and Clarke read them as testimony to character and Ellicott infers from them what must have been reported to the Council

Who may judge a controversy of doctrine: Calvin returns to the question at the reading of the letter, holding that judgment is properly referred to the learned and godly while the whole multitude is rightly admitted to hear the result

Clarke's argument that Judas and Silas were sent so that the letter could not be thought forged
Robertson's judgement that in comparison with the freedom won, the burden imposed is light
