31.pericope_label: The letter received at Antioch, and the proposal of a second journey

schools.summary: Gill notes that it was the brethren of the church at Antioch who read the letter delivered to them, and not Paul and Barnabas or Judas and Silas who were sent with it. By prophets he says are meant not only such as had the gift of foretelling things to come. Of the length of the stay he says how long is not certain, the Arabic version rendering it a year, which he thinks probable enough, that they might stay until things were thoroughly settled. The verse about Silas he treats as text and explains it: though Silas had leave to go and was actually dismissed with Judas, and doubtless intended to go with him, for some reason or another he changed his mind and stayed. Of the preaching at Antioch he says they preached the Gospel of Christ, not the word of men but the word of the Lord, of which he is both author and subject, and that they preached it in season and out of season. Calvin raises the difficulty that, seeing the epistle is so short and contains nothing but a bare narration, it is hard to see what consolation they could have by it, and answers that there was no small matter of consolation therein once they knew what had been determined. The two brethren, he says, were sent for this cause, that they might also testify by word the same thing which was contained in the letters, and more also, since otherwise the apostles would not have sent such short letters concerning so weighty a matter. Of the departure he says the brethren in taking their leave did wish them well, as friends use to do, and notes that only one of the two returned to Jerusalem. On the proposal of a second journey he marks first how careful Paul was for the churches he had ordained: he laboured at Antioch profitably, but because he remembered that he was an apostle ordained of God, and not the pastor of one particular place, he kept the course of his calling.

Henry sets the two halves of the chapter against each other: we have seen one unhappy difference among the brethren, which was of a public nature, brought to a good issue, but here we have a private quarrel between two ministers, no less men than Paul and Barnabas, not compromised indeed, yet ending well; and he begins with the good proposal Paul made to Barnabas to go and visit the churches they had planted.

Clarke says it was no matter of small moment to have a question on which such stress was laid decided by an apostolic council over which the Spirit of God presided. Prophets he takes in the sense often seen before, of teachers in the Church, who exhorted the brethren to abide steadily in the faith. Of the departure he says both had liberty to depart, but Silas chose to stay a little longer with the brethren; and of the verse that records the choice he says it is wanting in a great number of manuscripts, with the Syriac, Arabic, Coptic, Slavonic and Vulgate versions and some of the fathers, and does not appear to have been originally in the text. The proposal of a second journey he expands into an itinerary, since this heavenly man projected a journey to Cyprus, Pamphylia, Pisidia, Lycaonia and the cities where he had preached and founded churches in the preceding year. Wesley says that during the stay at Antioch Peter came down from Jerusalem and Paul withstood him to the face for separating himself from the Gentiles; and of the proposal that this was all Paul designed at first, but not all that God designed by his journey, whose providence carried him much farther than he intended, the seeing how they do meaning how their souls prosper and how they grow in faith.

Barnes says the brethren acquiesced in the decision of the apostles and elders and rejoiced that they were not to be subjected to the burdensome rites and ceremonies of the Jewish religion. Being prophets, he says, evidently implies that Judas and Silas had been preachers before they went to Antioch, though what the precise nature of the office of a prophet in the Christian church was is not easy to ascertain. Of the leave-taking he says the expression implies that they departed with the affectionate regard of the Christians to whom they had ministered. The verse recording that Silas remained he says is wanting in many manuscripts and in the Syriac, Arabic and Coptic versions, and is regarded as spurious by Mill, Griesbach and other critics, having probably been introduced by some early transcriber. Of the stay at Antioch he says how long is unknown, and that it is probable that at this time the unhappy incident occurred between Paul and Peter which is recorded in Galatians. Ellicott observes that the letter was probably read out by one who was himself emphatically the son of consolation in all the manifold aspects of that word, and that the verb rendered exhorted is the one from which the Greek for consolation was formed and includes that meaning here, this being the chief end to which the gift was directed. The better manuscripts, he says, have simply to those that had sent them and omit the verse about Silas, which was probably added by a later copyist to explain the fact mentioned a few verses later. Among the many others who taught at Antioch he would fairly reckon the prophets named earlier in the book, and, looking to the later history of the Church of Antioch, thinks it not improbable that we may think also of the martyr Ignatius. The commonly received chronology, he adds, makes the interval between the Council of Jerusalem and the second missionary journey somewhat more than a year, and the proposal to go again was characteristic of one whose heart was ever full of care for the churches. Robertson notes that the reading of the letter was public, to the church, and that the rejoicing is an ingressive aorist; the two men he calls forth-speakers for Christ who justify the commendation given them in the letter. The verse about Silas he says is not in the Revised Version or in the text of Westcott and Hort, being absent from the chief uncials and the Vulgate, and is clearly an addition. The stay he renders as having done time, how long we do not know; the season at Antioch he calls a time of general revival, naturally so after the victory at Jerusalem, and places the sad incident of Galatians at this point. In the proposal that follows he sees Paul taking the initiative as the leader, all the more so if the rebuke to Peter and Barnabas had already taken place, and being anxious, like a true missionary, to go back to the fields where he had laboured.

Chrysostom bids us observe again their humility, in that they let others also take part in the preaching, and passes at once to the proposal that they should go again and visit their brethren in every city where they had preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.

debates: Whether the verse recording that Silas stayed behind belongs to the text: Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Ellicott all reject it on manuscript evidence, Ellicott adding that a copyist probably supplied it to explain how Silas came to be at hand later, while Gill treats it as text and explains Silas's change of mind

How so bare a letter could console: Calvin raises the difficulty himself and answers that the consolation lay in knowing what had been determined, Clarke finds it in the authority of the council, Barnes in the relief from burdensome ceremonies, and Ellicott in the man who probably read it aloud

What the title prophet means here: Barnes says it implies previous preaching but confesses the office hard to define, Clarke reduces it to teaching, Gill warns against confining it to prediction, and Robertson calls them forth-speakers for Christ

Where the quarrel with Peter at Antioch belongs: Barnes, Robertson and Wesley all place it in this interval, Robertson drawing from it a reason why Paul takes the initiative in the proposal that follows

Why the two messengers were sent when a letter had been written: Calvin argues that they were to testify by word what the letter contained and more, since so short a letter would not otherwise have been sent on so weighty a matter
outliers: Ellicott's suggestion that the letter was read aloud by Barnabas, the son of consolation
Ellicott's conjecture that the martyr Ignatius may be among the many others who taught at Antioch

Wesley's remark that the journey Paul designed was not the journey God designed, providence carrying him much farther than he intended

Robertson's description of the season at Antioch as a time of general revival after the victory at Jerusalem

37.pericope_label: The quarrel over Mark and the parting of Paul and Barnabas

schools.summary: Gill says Barnabas consulted and contrived in his own mind and purposed within himself, though the Alexandrian copy and two of Beza's, with the Vulgate Latin, Syriac and Ethiopic versions, read that he would or was willing, having a great desire to take Mark. Of Paul's refusal he says he did not think Mark worthy, or a fit and proper person to go with them, as the word used seems to signify, and that the Syriac version renders it simply that Paul would not take him. In Mark's favour, he allows, it might be urged that his mother Mary was an excellent good woman who had received the saints into her house in a time of danger. Of the choice of Silas he says this was the design of the Holy Ghost in inclining his mind to stay longer at Antioch after he had been dismissed with Judas; and of the last journey that Antioch was the metropolis of Syria and Tarsus, the apostle's native place, was in Cilicia, and that he had been in both countries before and had been the instrument of converting many souls there. Calvin says Luke sets down here that doleful disagreement which ought to make all the godly afraid for just causes: the society of Paul and Barnabas was consecrated by the heavenly oracle, and they had long laboured, being of one mind, under the yoke to which the Lord had tied them, having proved by many experiences that God was with them.

Clarke says John Mark was the sister's son of Barnabas, and that natural affection might have led him to the partiality here mentioned. Of the contention he shows how little the Greek contains, since for the whole clause there stands only that there was therefore a paroxysm, an incitement, a stirring up, from a verb compounded of an intensive particle and a verb meaning to whet or sharpen. Of the commendation of Paul and Silas he reports that much stress has been laid upon it, to show that Barnabas was in the wrong and Paul in the right, because the brethren recommended Paul and Silas to the grace of God but did not so recommend Barnabas, and he doubts that the words will bear the weight. The confirming of the churches he calls the object of the journey, since they were young converts who had need of establishment, and there is no doubt that by showing them the decision made at the late council of Jerusalem their faith was greatly strengthened. Wesley says Barnabas counselled to take John because he was his kinsman, and that Paul thought it not right to trust again one who had deserted them before and had shrunk from the labour and danger of converting those they were now going to confirm. Of the contention he says it was literally a paroxysm, or fit of a fever, but that nothing in the text implies the sharpness was on both sides; it is far more probable that it was not, and that Paul, who had the right on his side as he undoubtedly had, maintained it with love. He notes besides that we do not find Barnabas stayed to be recommended by the brethren to the grace of God, and exclaims at the might of that grace in the midst of the world and of sin.

Barnes says the Greek of the first verb is willed or was disposed, that Mark had been with them before as a travelling companion, that he was the son of a sister of Barnabas, and that it is probable Barnabas's affection for his nephew was the reason of his wish. Paul, he says, did not think it proper, because he could not confide in Mark's perseverance with them in the toils and perils of their journey; why Mark had left them before is not known, but it was evidently for some cause which Paul did not consider satisfactory. The word rendered contention he says is that from which our word paroxysm is derived, and may denote any excitement of mind, being used in a good sense in the Epistle to the Hebrews, though here it evidently means a violent altercation which resulted in their separation for a time. Being recommended he glosses as being commended by prayer to God; and confirming the churches as strengthening them by instruction and exhortation, with no reference to the rite of confirmation. Ellicott says the Greek verb is hardly so strong as determined and prefers was minded, and that the ties of relationship led the uncle, or cousin, to wish to make another trial of his kinsman's fitness, since he saw extenuating circumstances which Paul could not recognise. The contention he renders literally as a sharp contention or paroxysm, and explains its heat by the warmth of previous affection, of a friendship begun probably in boyhood and cemented by new hopes and a great work in which both were sharers. From the choice of Silas he argues that, even if the verse about his remaining be rejected as an interpolation, it is clear he had remained when the other delegates from the Church of Jerusalem went back, which was in itself a proof of his interest in the mission-work among the Gentiles. On the last verse he notes that Cilicia had not been visited on the first journey with Barnabas, so that the churches there must have been founded at some earlier period, probably during Paul's residence at Tarsus before he came to Antioch; and that while confirming is used in the general sense of strengthening, the bestowal of spiritual gifts by the laying on of hands being a chief part of the work so done, it at least approximates to the idea of confirming in the later and more technical sense of the term. Robertson insists on the imperfect middle against the aorist middle of the received text, so that Barnabas willed, wished and stuck to it, and renders Paul's refusal by the imperfect of a verb meaning to think meet or right. The contention he calls our very word paroxysm, from a verb meaning to sharpen as of a blade and of the spirit, and remarks that this son of consolation loses his temper in a dispute over his cousin. Silas he says was chosen for himself as the successor of Barnabas, not of Mark, who had no place in Paul's plans at this time; and Paul took the opposite course from the first tour, going forth on his second mission tour with heart-aches and high hopes mingled together.

debates: Whether the sharpness lay on both sides: Wesley denies that anything in the text implies it and holds that Paul, having the right, maintained it with love, while Robertson says flatly that the son of consolation lost his temper, Barnes calls it a violent altercation, and Calvin treats the disagreement itself as a warning to the godly

Whether the narrative takes Paul's side: Clarke reports the argument from the brethren commending Paul and Silas and not Barnabas, and doubts the words will bear it, while Wesley presses the same silence as telling against Barnabas

What the verb rendered determined implies: Gill reports versions reading he would or was willing, Ellicott says the Greek is hardly so strong and prefers was minded, and Robertson insists on an imperfect against the received aorist, making Barnabas persist in the wish

Whether confirming carries any technical sense: Barnes denies that it has any reference to the rite of confirmation, while Ellicott allows the general sense of strengthening but holds that the laying on of hands makes the word approximate to the later technical meaning

Why Paul refused Mark: Barnes rests it on distrust of his perseverance and confesses that the cause of the earlier departure is unknown, Wesley on the desertion itself, and Gill on the sense of the word, that Paul did not think him a fit person
